summary: This unit teaches you to respond to a machine breakdown in a fabrication shop or plant and to lead a small team through the repair: making the area safe, working under a permit, isolating and locking off every energy source, finding the real cause by a logical method, repairing or replacing parts correctly, carrying out weld repairs on machines without harming them, testing and handing the machine back, and writing a report that helps stop the same breakdown happening again.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). When a machine stops, production stops: a press brake, an ironworker, a saw, a conveyor, a fume fan or a compressor. Everyone wants it running again quickly, and that pressure is exactly when people take short cuts and get hurt. A Level 3 welder-fitter must be able to get the machine going again **safely**, **properly** and **for good**.

You will often be the person who welds the broken bracket, guard or frame, so this unit also covers weld repairs on machines. Electrical faults are for the licensed electrician: your job is to recognise them, keep clear and work with the electrician.
**Who it is for:** Level 3 trainees and welder-fitters who are called to breakdowns of workshop machines and plant, and who lead or work in a small breakdown team.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Respond to the call
Make the area safe, help anyone hurt, get the operator's account, look without touching, and tell production what you know.
Work under a permit
Get a permit to work (and a hot work permit where needed) from the authorised person, and keep to it.
Isolate and lock off
Stop, isolate every energy source, fit personal locks and tags, deal with stored energy, and prove the machine cannot move.
Find the fault
Use facts, the manual, the history and your senses, follow the drive, check simple causes first, and find the root cause.
Repair or replace
Choose a safe, approved repair; get the right parts; strip, label, reassemble, torque and align correctly.
Weld on machines safely
Plan the weld, protect bearings, electronics, hoses and cables, prevent fire, and get approval for any change.
Test and hand back
Refit guards, remove your own lock, test run, check with the operator, and sign off the permit.
Report and prevent
Write a breakdown report with the cause and downtime, work out repair figures, and recommend changes to stop a repeat.
Lead the team
Brief the team, share tasks by skill, keep production informed, supervise trainees, and refuse short cuts.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on the first response, permits, isolation and lock-off, stored energy, fault-finding, repair decisions, welding on plant, parts, reassembly, return to service, reports, calculations, prevention and leading the team.
A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms (for example permit to work, hasp, stored energy, torque wrench, downtime, dial indicator, MTBF) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: a planned breakdown response on a belt-driven training machine with a permit, group lock-off, fault-finding and repair; and a weld repair of a broken machine bracket under a hot work permit, with a downtime log and a report.

blocks.note: In both practicals, the assessor watches your safety steps as closely as your repair: the permit, your own lock and tag, proving the machine will not start, refitting guards, and removing only your own lock at the end.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **breakdown** is an unplanned stop because something has failed. It costs lost output, idle workers, late deliveries and sometimes damage to other parts. It can also hurt people: the failure itself may injure someone, and the rush to restart leads to short cuts.

head: Kind of maintenance
What it means
Good and bad points
rows: Breakdown (run to failure)
Repair a machine only when it fails
No planning needed, but stops come at the worst time, take longer, and can damage other parts or hurt people
Planned preventive
Service at set times or running hours, from the maker's manual: greasing, oil changes, belt checks, inspections
Costs time and parts in advance, but stops are planned and short, and machines last longer
Condition-based (predictive)
Watch the machine's condition (temperature, vibration, noise, oil) and act when it starts to change
Catches failures early; needs regular checks and records
Improvement
Change the design or method so that a repeat fault cannot happen
Removes the cause for good; needs approval and sometimes money

flow: Go to the machine with your PPE and basic tools
Make the area safe: keep people back; look for anyone hurt, leaks, hot parts, trapped material and exposed live parts
If someone is hurt or trapped, give first aid if trained and call for help (in Jamaica, 110 for fire and ambulance)
Get the operator's account of what happened
Look, listen and smell from outside, without touching moving parts or opening guards
Read the maintenance history and the maker's manual
Tell the production supervisor what you know and a first estimate of time
Arrange the permit, then isolate and lock off before any hands-on work

ul: What was the machine doing, and what material or job was on it?
What happened just before it stopped? Any noise, smell, smoke, vibration, warning light or alarm?
Has it done this before? Has anything been changed recently (blade, tooling, settings, operator)?
What did you do after it stopped? Did you reset anything or try to restart it?

blocks.p: The operator's account gives you clues that save time, and you need it for the report. Ask to understand, not to find someone to blame: an operator who fears blame will not tell you the useful part.

blocks.note: Never restart a broken machine "to hear the fault". Never keep resetting a tripped overload or breaker: a trip is a symptom that something is drawing too much current. Resetting it again and again can burn out the motor and hides the cause. Isolate the machine, find out why it tripped, and leave the electrical side to the electrician.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Power cuts, dips and surges, especially in the thunderstorm season, can trip machines or damage their electronics, so a machine that stopped during an outage may have no mechanical fault at all. Machines should have a **no-volt release**, which stops them restarting by themselves when the power returns. Never bypass it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A **permit to work (PTW)** is a signed, written system that controls high-risk work such as breakdown repairs on plant. It makes sure the right people know what is being done, that the machine has been made safe, and that it is not restarted until the work is finished and everyone is clear.

head: A permit to work states
Why
rows: The machine and its location
So there is no doubt which machine is being worked on
The work to be done
Work outside this scope needs a new or changed permit
The hazards
So everyone knows what could hurt them
The isolations made, where, and who locked them
So they can be checked, and removed only at the end
Other precautions
PPE, barriers, a hot work permit, a gas test, a standby person
The time and date it is valid
Work stops when the permit runs out, until it is renewed
The names of the people authorised to work
Only they may do the work
Signatures for issue, acceptance, hand-back and cancellation
A clear record of who handed what to whom

ul: Only **authorised persons** (trained and named in writing by the site) issue permits or carry out work under them. Knowing the machine well, or owning the right tools, does not make someone authorised.
Other permits may be needed with it: a **hot work permit** for welding, cutting or grinding; a confined space permit; a permit for work at height.
If the job changes, the conditions change or the time runs out, stop and go back to the person who issued the permit.

blocks.h: Isolation and lock-off, step by step

flow: Find every energy source from the manual and drawings: electrical, hydraulic, pneumatic, gravity, springs, moving parts, heat
Tell the operator and anyone affected that the machine is being isolated
Stop the machine with its normal controls
Isolate each energy source at its isolator: the electrical isolator, the air valve, the hydraulic supply
Each person working fits his or her own padlock and danger tag to each isolation point, using a multi-lock hasp
Release or restrain stored energy: lower or block raised parts, bleed pressure, wait for moving parts to stop
Prove it: with everyone clear, try the start controls, then return them to off; the electrician proves the electrical supply dead with a tester checked before and after use
Record the isolations on the permit; only then start work

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Isolator
A switch or valve that cuts the machine off from its energy supply and can be locked in the off position
Stop button
A control, not an isolation. The machine can be started again by someone else, or by a fault in the control circuit
Multi-lock hasp
A clip with holes for several padlocks; the isolator cannot be switched on until the last lock is removed
Personal padlock
A lock with one key, kept by its owner, so nobody else can remove it
Danger tag
A label on the lock giving the person's name, the date, the reason and how to contact them
Prove (try)
Testing that the machine really cannot start or move after isolation

ul: Every person working fits his or her own lock, so that the machine cannot be switched on while **anyone** is still working on it. One shared lock, or one person "standing by the switch", is not enough.
Only the person who fitted a lock removes it, at the end of his or her own work.
At a shift change, the incoming person fits his or her lock **before** the outgoing person removes theirs.

If a lock is left on and its owner has gone (an **abandoned lock**), it is removed only by the person in charge, following the site's written procedure: confirm the owner is not on site and try to contact them, check the machine is safe and everyone is clear, then record it.

Electrical work (testing, wiring, motors, controls, fuses) is done only by the licensed electrician. A fitter who finds burnt wiring stops and calls the electrician; never tape wires or fit a bigger fuse.

blocks.note: "Skip the lock-off just this once, it's a quick job" is how people lose fingers and hands. Refuse, politely and firmly, and isolate and lock off as normal, however senior the person asking.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Stored energy** is energy left in a machine after its supply has been isolated. It can still make parts move, fall, spring or spray. Locking the isolator does not remove it: you must release it or hold it safely.

head: Kind
Examples in a fabrication shop
How to make it safe
rows: Gravity
Press brake beam, ironworker or press ram, raised saw head, guillotine blade, a load on a hoist
Lower it fully to its rest, or hold it with the maker's safety blocks or rated props. Never rely on hydraulics or on someone watching
Hydraulic pressure
Cylinders, accumulators, hoses and valves
Release it as the manual says, through the bleed or release valve, and check the gauge reads zero before opening anything
Compressed air
Air receivers, lines, clamp cylinders on jigs
Close and lock the supply valve, bleed the line through the dump valve, check the gauge reads zero
Moving parts
Flywheels on shears and punches, saw blades, fans and motors running down
Wait until they have stopped completely, and check by looking and listening
Springs and tension
Bandsaw blade tension, spring clamps, belt tensioners, counterbalance springs
Release the tension with the proper adjuster, or restrain the spring, as the manual says
Electrical charge
Capacitors in variable speed drives, inverters and welding machines
Wait the time on the warning label; the electrician proves it dead
Heat
Hot oil, motors, bearings, recently welded parts
Let it cool and check the temperature before handling

blocks.note: A pinhole leak in a hydraulic hose can inject oil through the skin. It may feel like only a sting, but it is a serious emergency: go to hospital at once and say it is an injection injury. **Never feel for a hydraulic leak with your hand.** Look for it with a piece of card held at arm's length, with eye protection, or better, release the pressure first.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: A hydraulic ram or beam can drift down after isolation, because oil slowly leaks past valves and seals. That is why blocks are used, not trust.
Use the maker's safety blocks or props rated for the load. A piece of timber picked up in the yard may split.
When a bandsaw blade is removed, release its tension first: a tensioned blade can whip or snap when freed. Wear gloves and eye protection when handling blades.

blocks.p: Changing parts until the machine works wastes time and money, can add new faults, and often leaves the real cause in place. A **logical method** finds the real cause quickly.

flow: Collect the facts: the operator's account, the history, the manual
With the machine isolated, look, listen, feel and smell
Understand the system: follow the power from the motor through belts, chains, gearbox and shafts to the tool
Check the simple, likely causes first
Split the system into parts and test each one to narrow the search
Confirm the cause before you replace anything
Ask why it happened, until you reach the root cause
Record what you found

head: Sense
What it can tell you
rows: Look
Oil leaks, loose or broken parts, cracks, wear, belt dust, blue (overheated) metal, misalignment, missing keys or bolts
Listen (while running, before isolation, or in the test run)
Squeal: a belt slipping. Knock: something loose or broken. Rumble or grinding: a bearing. Hiss: an air leak. Whine: gears or a pump
Feel (isolated, and with care)
Heat in bearings, motors and gearboxes; play in shafts and bearings; tension in belts and chains. An infra-red thermometer is safer and gives a figure to compare
Smell
Burnt rubber: a belt slipping. Burnt varnish: motor windings overheating (call the electrician). Hot oil: a gearbox or hydraulic system running hot

head: Part
Signs
Likely causes
What to do
rows: Rolling bearings
Noise, heat, vibration, play
Too little or too much grease, dirt or water, misalignment, belts too tight, welding current passed through it
Fit the correct bearing; fix the cause; grease to the schedule, with the right amount
V-belts
Squeal, slip, burnt smell, cracks, shiny (glazed) sides, black dust
Too loose, worn, oily, pulleys out of line, worn pulley grooves
Tension to the maker's figure; replace as a matched set; align the pulleys
Chains and sprockets
Jumping teeth, noise, stiff links
Stretched chain, hooked sprocket teeth, misalignment, poor lubrication, wrong tension
Replace the chain (and the sprockets if worn); align; tension; lubricate
Gearboxes
Noise, heat, oil leaks
Low or wrong oil, worn gears or bearings, failed seals, overload
Correct oil grade and level from the manual; repair or replace parts
Couplings and keys
Knocking; motor turns but the tool does not
Misalignment, wear, a sheared key, overload
Align; fit a key of the correct size and material
Shear pins and slip clutches
The drive stops suddenly
A jam or overload: the pin has done its job of protecting the drive
Clear the jam, find the overload, fit the **correct** pin
Hydraulics
Slow or weak, leaks, overheating, noisy pump
Low oil, blocked filter, worn pump, leaking seals, damaged hose
Follow the manual's fault chart
Fasteners
Loose or broken bolts
Vibration, wrong grade or torque, fatigue
Correct grade, torque and locking method; find the source of the vibration

blocks.note: A shear pin that keeps breaking is telling you the drive keeps being overloaded or jammed. Never fit a stronger bolt or pin in its place: the next overload will break something far more expensive, or hurt someone. Find the overload.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **The maker's service manual:** how the machine works, settings, tightening torques, fitting order, clearances, oil grades, fault-finding charts, parts lists.
**The maintenance history (log):** repeat faults point to the real cause. Three bearing failures in a year is a pattern, not bad luck.
**Drawings and parts lists:** part numbers and how assemblies fit together.
**The operator and other fitters:** what they have seen before.
**The maker or supplier:** technical help for unusual faults.

blocks.p: Fixing the broken part is fixing the symptom. Ask "why?" until you reach a cause that, once fixed, stops it happening again. For example: the bearing failed because it overheated; it overheated because the belts were far too tight; the belts were too tight because nobody had the tension figure; nobody had it because the manual was never used for belt changes. Fit the bearing, **and** set the tension from the manual and add it to the maintenance sheet.

ul: Will the repair restore the part to full strength and safe working? If not, replace it.
What does the maker say? Some parts (cast iron housings, hardened shafts, pressure parts, lifting parts) should not be welded except to an **approved procedure**, or not at all.
Compare the cost and time of a repair with a new part, and the cost of the downtime while you wait.
Cast iron cracks easily when welded. It needs special electrodes (often nickel-based), careful preheat and slow cooling, done to an approved procedure by a skilled welder, or the part is replaced.
A load-bearing or safety part is repaired only with the approval of the person in charge, and the repair is inspected.

blocks.p: A **temporary repair** keeps a machine running safely until a proper repair can be made, for example while the right part is on order. It is acceptable only when it is:

ul: **Safe:** it does not remove a guard or safety device, overload any part, or make the machine behave unpredictably.
**Approved** by the person in charge, such as the maintenance supervisor.
**Marked:** tagged on the machine as temporary, with any limits (lower speed, lighter load) explained to the operator.
**Recorded** in the breakdown report and maintenance log, with the date the permanent repair is due.
**Followed up:** the correct part is ordered at once, the temporary repair is checked often, and the record is closed when the permanent repair is made.

blocks.p: A temporary repair is never acceptable just because production is behind, the operator agrees, or the right part is expensive.

ul: Read the part number from the old part or from the parts list for your exact model. A description such as "the small bearing" is not enough.
Use only the correct part, or one the maker or engineer has approved as equal: same sizes, rating, material and, for hoses and fittings, a **working pressure at least as high** as the machine's.
A part that "nearly fits", packed out with shims or forced in, will fail early and may damage the machine.

head: Bearing marking
What it means
rows: The first digit (6) is the type: deep-groove ball bearing. The second (2) is the size series. The last two digits give the bore: from 04 upwards, multiply by 5, so 05 = 25 mm bore. (00 = 10 mm, 01 = 12 mm, 02 = 15 mm, 03 = 17 mm)
2RS (or 2RS1)
Rubber seals on both sides
ZZ (or 2Z)
Metal shields on both sides
C3
More internal clearance than normal, for bearings that run hot or have a tight fit

ul: Take photos before and during the strip-down.
Mark mating parts (match marks) so they go back the same way round.
Lay the parts out **in order** on a clean bench, and label and bag small parts and fasteners with the part they came from.
Note the position and thickness of any shims and spacers.
Clean and inspect each part, and measure wear against the limits in the manual.
Fit new seals and gaskets; never re-use a damaged one.
Tighten bolts with a **torque wrench** to the figure in the manual, in the order it gives. Torque = force × distance: a 60 N·m bolt needs 200 N on the end of a 0.3 m spanner (60 ÷ 0.3).

Align pulleys with a straight edge or a tight string across both pulley faces (or a laser tool). Align shafts and couplings with a **dial indicator** (dial gauge) or a laser tool, to the manual's limits. Misalignment wears bearings, belts and couplings early.
Tension belts to the maker's figure or gauge. A common guide is a deflection of about 16 mm per metre of span under the test force the maker gives.
Replace V-belts as a **matched set**: a new belt beside a stretched old one carries most of the load and fails early.
Fill gearboxes and hydraulic tanks with the oil **grade** in the manual, to the correct **level**. The wrong oil or level can wreck gears and bearings within hours.
Refit every guard before any test run.

blocks.p: Many breakdowns end with a weld: a cracked bracket, a broken guard mounting, a torn frame. Welding on or near a machine has hazards and risks of damage that welding on the bench does not.

flow: The machine is isolated and locked off under the permit, and a hot work permit is issued
Check what is nearby: belts, hydraulic hoses, grease and oil, plastic covers, cables, electronics, wood, dust and rubbish
Remove what can burn, or shield it with welding blankets; clean off oil and grease
Identify the material and decide the method; get approval if the part carries load or the design changes
Prepare the joint: grind out any crack to sound metal and check it has gone (for example with dye penetrant)
Fix the work return clamp on the part being welded, right next to the weld
Protect electronics as the maker says (the electrician may need to disconnect drives, sensors or controllers)
Put up screens; a fire watcher with an extinguisher stands by; weld
Clean and inspect the weld; the fire watch stays for the time the hot work permit sets
Refit parts and guards, test, and record the repair

blocks.p: Welding current flows from the electrode to the work return clamp by the easiest path. If the clamp is far from the weld, the current may pass through parts that it damages:

ul: **Bearings:** current arcs between the balls or rollers and the races, pitting them. The damage shows up later as noise and early failure.
**Chains, gears and couplings:** arcing pits the contact faces.
**Hydraulic cylinder rods:** arcing damages the hard chrome surface and then the seals.
**Control cables, sensors and drives:** stray current can destroy electronics.
**Building steel, pipes and earth wires:** stray current can heat connections and start fires.

blocks.note: Fix the work return clamp on the **part being welded**, on clean metal, as close to the weld as possible, so the current cannot pass through bearings, chains or controls. Never clamp to a control panel, a guard on another part, or the building steel.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Spatter can burn through a hydraulic hose in seconds and spray oil into the arc, causing a fierce fire. Shield hoses with welding blankets, or remove them, and keep a fire watch.
PVC cable insulation melts and burns, giving off harmful smoke. Cover cable trays near the work.
Sparks lodge in wooden pallets, rags, oily dust and gaps in floors and smoulder for a long time. Move combustibles well away and check below and behind the work.

Find out why the part cracked. A **fatigue** crack (often starting at the toe of an old weld or a sharp corner) comes from vibration or repeated loading: if the cause is left (a loose mounting, an out-of-balance part, an overload), the repair will crack again.
Adding a gusset, changing a plate thickness or moving a mounting changes the design. Get approval from the person in charge first, and record the change.
Welding on shafts, hardened parts and cast iron is high risk: they can crack or distort. Use an approved procedure or replace the part.
Inspect the finished weld (size, profile, no cracks or undercut), and check the repaired part is secure before the guard goes back.

flow: Check the work is complete and nothing is left loose
Remove tools, rags and spare parts from the machine; count the tools
Refit every guard and safety device, and check they work
Check fluid levels, belt and chain tension, and that bolts are torqued
Count the team: everyone clear of the machine; area tidy
Each person removes only his or her own lock and tag
The authorised person restores the supplies in the right order
Test run: slowly and without load first, then with a test piece; watch for leaks, noise, heat and vibration
Check the emergency stop and interlocks work
The operator checks the output (for example a test cut or bend)
Sign off and return the permit; tell the supervisor; write the report

blocks.p: If anything is wrong during the test run (a new knock, a leak, a hot bearing), **stop, isolate again** and find the cause. Never hand over a machine "to see if the noise goes away", and never add grease or adjust parts while it is running. The test run has the same hazards as normal use, which is why the guards go back on first.

head: Section
What to write
Why it matters
rows: Machine
Name, number, location
So the records build a history for each machine
Times
When it stopped, when it restarted, the downtime
For cost and reliability figures
Symptoms
What the operator saw and heard
Clues for next time
Fault and root cause
What failed and why
So the same failure can be prevented, not only repaired
Work done
Repairs, adjustments, parts and materials used (with part numbers), who did the work
For stores, costs and the next repair
Temporary repairs
What is temporary, its limits and the date for the permanent repair
So it is not forgotten
Safety issues and recommendations
For example more frequent greasing, a guard change, operator training
To stop the next breakdown

ul: **Downtime:** a machine stopped at 10:25 and restarted at 14:05 was down 3 h 40 min = 220 minutes.
**Cost of lost output:** downtime in hours × the value lost per hour. At J$36 000 an hour, 3 h 40 min (3.67 h) costs about J$132 000.
**MTBF (mean time between failures)** = running hours ÷ number of failures. 3 failures in 960 running hours: MTBF = 320 hours. A higher MTBF means a more reliable machine.
**MTTR (mean time to repair)** = total repair time ÷ number of repairs. Repairs of 2, 3.5 and 2.5 hours: MTTR = 8 ÷ 3 = 2.67 h, about 2 h 40 min.
**Re-order level for a spare** = use per month × months the supplier takes + safety stock. A belt used twice a month, with a 3-month delivery and a safety stock of 2: re-order at 2 × 3 + 2 = 8.
**Torque** = force × distance (N × m = N·m).

sections.title: Leading the team and preventing repeats

ul: **Brief** the team before work: the fault, the permit, the isolations, the hazards, the plan and each person's task.
Check that each person has the right PPE and has fitted a personal lock and tag.
Share tasks by skill: for example one strips and labels parts, one checks the drive and alignment, the licensed electrician deals with anything electrical.

A trainee works **under supervision** on tasks that suit a learner: laying out and labelling parts, cleaning, fetching parts, recording. A trainee never removes other people's locks, signs a permit or does electrical tests alone.
Keep the work area tidy, and watch for short cuts, such as reaching under a raised part that is not blocked.
Keep the production supervisor informed: give the likely repair time as soon as you know it, and update it at once if it changes, so production can plan round the downtime.
Arrange parts quickly; if the right part is not available, discuss a safe, approved temporary repair or the wait.
At the end, make sure everyone is clear before locks come off, lead the test run, then debrief the team and write the report.

blocks.p: Production losses are real and you should work quickly, but never by skipping a safety step. When someone, however senior, asks you to skip the lock-off, leave a guard off "for now" or restart before the test, refuse and explain why. Use the waiting time well (prepare parts, brief the team) so the job moves as fast as it safely can. Record serious pressure in your report.

ul: Keep a **planned maintenance** schedule for each machine, taken from the maker's manual: daily operator checks (oil, air, guards, unusual noise), weekly greasing and belt checks, and longer-interval inspections and oil changes.
Train operators to use the machine within its limits and to report early signs (noise, heat, leaks, vibration) instead of running until it stops.
Keep spares of parts that fail often, with re-order levels.

Record every breakdown and its root cause, and look at the records regularly: which machines fail most, which parts, and what the downtime costs. Change the planned maintenance where the records show a pattern.
Where a fault keeps coming back, consider an improvement: better alignment, a guard to stop a hose rubbing, a stronger mounting (with approval).
Used oil, old grease, oily rags and filters go into the marked containers for safe disposal or recycling by an approved contractor.
Never pour oil into a drain or onto the ground, and never burn rags in the scrap skip.
Clean up spills with the spill kit or absorbent at once: oil on the floor causes falls.
Leave the area as you found it, or better, before you hand the machine back.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor.

ul: I can make a breakdown area safe and get a useful account from the operator.
I can explain why a tripped overload must not simply be reset.
I can say what a permit to work contains and who may work under it.
I can isolate and lock off a machine with a personal lock and tag on a multi-lock hasp, and prove it cannot start.
I can explain why only the person who fitted a lock removes it, and how an abandoned lock is dealt with.
I can name the kinds of stored energy and make each one safe.
I can explain the danger of hydraulic injection and how to look for a leak safely.
I can find a fault by a logical method, using my senses, the manual and the history.
I can recognise common faults in bearings, belts, chains, gearboxes, couplings and hydraulics.
I can find the root cause of a repeat failure.
I can decide between repair and replacement, and control a temporary repair.
I can read a bearing number and order the right part.
I can strip down and reassemble parts in order, with the right torque, alignment, tension and oil.
I can plan a weld repair on a machine, placing the return clamp correctly and protecting hoses, cables and electronics.
I can test a repaired machine and hand it back under the permit.
I can write a breakdown report that helps prevent a repeat.
I can work out downtime, its cost, MTBF, MTTR, torque and re-order levels.
I can lead a small breakdown team, keep production informed and refuse short cuts.
I can compare breakdown and planned maintenance and suggest how to reduce breakdowns.
I can clear up and dispose of oil and waste safely.

terms: Abandoned lock
A personal lock left on an isolator after its owner has gone
Authorised person
Someone trained and named in writing to issue or work under a permit
Breakdown maintenance
Repairing a machine only after it fails
Danger tag
A label on a lock showing who fitted it, when and why
Dial indicator
A gauge with a needle on a round face, used to check run-out and alignment
Downtime
The time a machine is stopped and not producing
Fatigue crack
A crack that grows under vibration or repeated loading
Hasp
A clip with holes for many padlocks, so the isolator stays off until the last lock is removed
Hot work permit
A permit that controls welding, cutting and grinding
Isolator
A switch or valve that cuts off a machine's energy and can be locked off
Matched set
Belts of the same make and length, fitted together on one drive
MTBF
Mean time between failures: running hours ÷ number of failures
MTTR
Mean time to repair: total repair time ÷ number of repairs
No-volt release
A device that stops a machine restarting by itself when power returns
Permit to work (PTW)
The signed written system that controls high-risk work on plant
Planned (preventive) maintenance
Servicing at set intervals to stop failures happening
Prove (try)
Testing that an isolated machine really cannot start or move
Root cause
The underlying reason for a failure which, once fixed, stops it recurring
Safety block
A block placed in a press or brake to stop the ram or beam coming down
Service manual
The maker's book of repair steps, settings and parts
Shear pin
A pin designed to break under overload to protect a drive
Stored energy
Energy left in a machine after isolation, such as a raised ram or trapped pressure
Temporary repair
A safe, approved, recorded repair that keeps a machine running until a proper repair
Torque wrench
A wrench that tightens a bolt to a set value in newton metres
Work return clamp
The clamp that completes the welding circuit; fixed next to the weld

c1.title: A stalled bandsaw at a steel stockist in Kingston
c1.text: A large horizontal bandsaw at a steel stockist in Kingston stops part-way through cutting a beam. The operator, Marlon, says the blade slowed and squealed, there was a smell of burning rubber, then the motor stopped and the overload tripped. He has reset the overload twice and wants to try once more. He says the blade has not been changed for weeks and he turned the feed up to finish a big order. Shamar, a Level 3 welder-fitter, leads the repair with a helper; the stockist's licensed electrician is on call.

c2.title: A leaking ironworker in May Pen
c2.text: At a fabrication shop in May Pen, Clarendon, a hydraulic ironworker (a combined punch and shear) has stopped with its punch ram part-way down. Oil is misting from a small split in a hose beside the punch cylinder, and the operator, Tashana, offers to run her hand along the hose to find the exact spot. After the machine is isolated, its pressure gauge still reads 70 bar. The stores have a hose of the right length with the right end fittings, but its printed working pressure is lower than the machine's. The old hose has a worn patch where it rubbed against the frame.

c3.title: A noisy fume extraction fan in Port Maria
c3.text: At a training centre in Port Maria, St Mary, the belt-driven fan of the welding-fume extraction system has become noisy and vibrates. The records show its bearings have been replaced three times this year. The old bearing is marked 6206-2RS. The fitter finds the two V-belts very tight, one of them worn and cracked, and the motor pulley about 4 mm out of line with the fan pulley.

c4.title: A cracked motor bracket in Hayes
c4.text: At a steel fabrication shop in Hayes, Clarendon, the bracket that carries the drive motor of a powered roller table has cracked along the toe of an old weld, and the motor is sagging. The table is chain-driven and controlled by a variable speed drive with sensors. Below the bracket runs a tray of PVC-covered cables, and wooden pallets are stacked nearby. Dwayne plans to weld the bracket in place and would like to add a gusset so it does not crack again.

c5.title: The cold saw breakdown log in Brown's Town
c5.text: A fabrication shop in Brown's Town, St Ann, logs every breakdown of its cold saw. In the last 1 500 running hours it broke down 6 times, and the repairs took 2.5, 4, 1.5, 3, 4 and 3 hours. Four of the six faults were traced to low or wrong oil in the saw's gearbox. The saw uses about 4 blades a month, a blade order takes six weeks to arrive, and the shop wants a safety stock of 2 blades.

questions.q: Marlon wants to reset the overload once more to see if the saw will run. What should Shamar do?
o: Let him try once, standing well back from the blade
Reset it himself, since a fitter knows the saw better
Stop him, isolate the saw and find out why it tripped
Let him try, but with the feed turned down low
questions.why: An overload trip is a symptom: the motor was drawing too much current. Resetting it again and again can burn out the motor and hides the cause. Isolate, investigate, and leave the electrical checks to the electrician.

questions.q: Before taking the jammed blade off, what must Shamar do about it?
o: Cut through the blade with a grinder to free it quickly
Leave the tension on so that the blade stays in its guides
Release the blade tension first, as the manual says
Knock the blade out of the cut with a heavy mallet
questions.why: A tensioned bandsaw blade is stored energy: freed suddenly, it can whip or snap. Release the tension first, then handle the blade with gloves and eye protection.

questions.q: Which checks will most likely find why the blade stalled in the cut?
o: The paint on the saw frame and the bolts holding it down
The blade's condition and tension, and the feed setting
The lighting over the saw and the operator's choice of PPE
The length of the beam being cut and the size of the order
questions.why: A dull blade fed too hard binds in the cut, the drive belt slips and burns, and the motor overloads. The squeal, the burning rubber, the old blade and the raised feed all point there; fix the blade and feed, not just the belt.

questions.q: At the end of the day the helper's padlock is still on the hasp, and he has gone home with the key. What is right?
o: Shamar cuts the lock off himself, since he is leading the job
The person in charge follows the abandoned-lock procedure
The electrician removes it, as he was the one who isolated the supply
Marlon removes it with bolt cutters so the saw can run tomorrow
questions.why: Only a lock's owner removes it. When the owner has gone, the person in charge follows the written procedure: confirm he is not on site and try to reach him, check the machine is safe and clear, then remove the lock and record it.

questions.q: What should be said to Tashana's offer to find the leak with her hand?
o: Yes, as long as she is wearing thick leather welding gloves
No: oil from a pinhole can be injected through the skin
Yes, but only after the pump motor has been switched off
Yes, since a split as small as that can only drip oil
questions.why: High-pressure oil from a pinhole can pass through gloves and skin into the body: a serious injury that needs hospital treatment at once. Look for leaks with card, with pressure released where possible.

questions.q: The gauge still reads 70 bar after isolation. What must happen before the hose is disconnected?
o: Undo the fitting slowly so that the oil bleeds out gently
Wrap the fitting in a thick rag and then undo it quickly
Release it as the manual says and see the gauge read zero
Carry on, since 70 bar is low for a hydraulic machine
questions.why: Trapped pressure is stored energy. Release it by the method the maker gives, and check the gauge reads zero. The ram must also be supported, as it can drop when pressure goes.

questions.q: Can the hose from stores be used?
o: Yes, because its length and end fittings match the old hose
Yes, if two clips are fitted at each end for extra grip
Yes, as a stop-gap until a better hose comes next month
No: its rating must be at least the machine's pressure
questions.why: A hose rated below the working pressure can burst, spraying oil at high pressure. Use the correct part or an approved equal with a working pressure at least as high as the machine's.

questions.q: What recommendation should the breakdown report make?
o: Re-route, clamp and sleeve the hose so it cannot rub
Keep a spare hose hanging on the machine for next time
Tell operators to run the ironworker at a slower speed
Fit a stronger hose and leave it routed the same way
questions.why: The root cause was the hose rubbing on the frame. Re-routing, clamping and sleeving it stops the next failure; a spare or a stronger hose left in the same place only delays it.

questions.q: What does the marking 6206-2RS tell the fitter?
o: A ball bearing with a 62 mm bore and metal shields on both sides
A roller bearing 206 mm across, with a rust-resisting finish
A ball bearing with a 6 mm bore, made for two-speed motors
A deep-groove ball bearing, 30 mm bore, rubber seals both sides
questions.why: 6 is the deep-groove ball type, 2 the size series, and 06 × 5 gives a 30 mm bore. 2RS means rubber seals on both sides; metal shields would be ZZ or 2Z.

questions.q: How should the fitter stop the bearings failing again?
o: Fit a stronger type of bearing and keep plenty of spares in stores
Grease the bearings twice as often as the schedule says
Replace the whole fan unit, since it keeps on failing so often
Fix the belt tension and pulley line-up, then fit new bearings
questions.why: Over-tight belts and misaligned pulleys overload the bearings: that is the root cause of three failures. New bearings alone will fail again; extra grease can make them run hotter.

questions.q: How should the pulley line-up be checked?
o: By measuring from each pulley to the nearest wall
By sighting along the belts while the fan is running at full speed
With a straight edge or tight string across both pulley faces
With a spirit level laid on top of each pulley
questions.why: A straight edge, string line or laser across both faces shows any offset or angle between the pulleys. Walls are not a datum, a spirit level shows only level, and you never sight along a running drive.

questions.q: One belt is worn and cracked; the other looks fine. What should be fitted?
o: Two new belts as a matched set
One new belt beside the old one
One belt only, with the other left off
The worn belt turned inside out
questions.why: A new belt is shorter than a stretched one, so it carries most of the load and fails early. V-belts on one drive are replaced together as a matched set and tensioned to the maker's figure.

questions.q: Where should Dwayne fix the work return clamp?
o: On the bracket itself, close to the crack
On the roller table frame beside the motor
On the earth bar inside the drive panel
On the nearest steel column of the building
questions.why: On the part being welded, next to the weld, the current goes straight back to the machine. Further away it can pass through the chain, the motor bearings or the drive electronics and damage them, or heat other paths.

questions.q: How should the crack be prepared before welding?
o: Weld straight over it with a wider bead than before
Clean off the paint only, then fill the crack with weld
Seal the crack with epoxy filler, then weld over it
Grind it out to sound metal and check that it has gone
questions.why: Weld laid over a crack leaves the crack inside, ready to grow again. Grind until it has gone, check with dye penetrant or a magnifier, then weld into clean, sound metal.

questions.q: What should be done about the cable tray and the pallets?
o: Move the pallets away and cover the tray with welding blankets
Weld quickly, so that the sparks have no time to start a fire there
Soak the pallets and the cables with water before starting work
Leave them, as the hot work permit covers the fire risk
questions.why: Sparks lodge in wood and PVC melts and burns with harmful smoke. Remove what can be moved and shield what cannot; the permit lists these controls, it does not replace them. Water near live cables adds a shock risk.

questions.q: Dwayne wants to add a gusset to the bracket. What should he do first?
o: Add it, since a stronger bracket can only be an improvement
Get approval for the change, then record it in the report
Add it if the machine operator agrees that it looks right
Leave it out and lay a much heavier weld bead instead
questions.why: A gusset changes the design and can move the stress somewhere else. The person in charge approves design changes; the report records it, and also the cause of the cracking, such as vibration.

questions.q: What is the saw's mean time between failures (MTBF)?
o: 250 hours
300 hours
83 hours
9 000 hours
questions.why: MTBF = running hours ÷ number of failures = 1 500 ÷ 6 = 250 hours. A rising MTBF over the next months will show whether the improvements are working.

questions.q: What is the mean time to repair (MTTR)?
o: 18 hours
4 hours
3.6 hours
3 hours
questions.why: MTTR = total repair time ÷ number of repairs = (2.5 + 4 + 1.5 + 3 + 4 + 3) ÷ 6 = 18 ÷ 6 = 3 hours. Eighteen hours is the total, not the mean.

questions.q: At what stock level should the shop re-order blades?
o: 6 blades
4 blades
8 blades
26 blades
questions.why: Six weeks is 1.5 months, so use during delivery = 4 × 1.5 = 6 blades; add the safety stock of 2 to re-order at 8. Multiplying 4 a month by 6 weeks mixes up the units.

questions.q: What does the log suggest would cut breakdowns the most?
o: Keeping more spare blades in stores so that repairs are quicker
Gearbox oil checks in planned maintenance, and operator training
Buying a new saw, as this one keeps on breaking down every month
Logging only the big faults from now on, to save time on paperwork
questions.why: Four of six failures share one root cause: gearbox oil. Regular checks of oil level and grade from the manual, and operators trained to report early signs, remove that cause. The log is how the pattern was found.
